stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 attends her 28-week antenatal appointment after a routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She has been well throughout pregnancy with a normal 20-week morphology scan and appropriate fundal height. Her BMI at booking was 27 kg/m2 and her father has type 2 diabetes.

Her results are fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L, one-hour glucose 10.4 mmol/L and two-hour glucose 7.9 mmol/L. She reports no polyuria or polydipsia and her home glucose monitoring since triage has shown fasting values ranging from 4.6 to 4.9 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm at 28 weeks, longitudinal cephalic presentation, fetal movements normal
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.2 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 7.9 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4 percent (below 5.7)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic interpretation and next step?

options.text: GDM diagnosed on fasting glucose criterion, refer for immediate insulin commencement
options.rationale: Fasting is below the ADIPS 5.1 mmol/L threshold; the diagnosis is made on the 1 hour value alone. (Source: ADIPS GDM Consensus 2014)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

options.text: GDM diagnosed on the 1 hour value; start lifestyle plus home glucose monitoring
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria: fasting 5.1 or above, 1 hour 10.0 or above, or 2 hour 8.5 or above; the 1 hour of 10.4 meets threshold; lifestyle plus monitoring is initial management. (Source: ADIPS GDM Consensus 2014)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

options.text: Normal test; reassure and no further monitoring or intervention required in this pregnancy
options.rationale: The 1 hour value 10.4 is above the ADIPS 10.0 threshold, so this cannot be labelled as normal. (Source: ADIPS GDM Consensus 2014)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

options.text: Overt diabetes in pregnancy; refer for endocrinology-led insulin initiation this week
options.rationale: Overt diabetes is fasting 7.0 or above, random 11.1 or above, or HbA1c 6.5 or above; this OGTT does not meet those criteria. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance; repeat 75 g OGTT in four weeks with same thresholds applied
options.rationale: IGT is not the ADIPS diagnostic category in pregnancy; the OGTT is not repeated when a threshold is already crossed. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

explanation.summary: ADIPS 2014 criteria for GDM use fasting 5.1 or above, one-hour 10.0 or above, or two-hour 8.5 or above (any one criterion suffices). Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting 7.0 or above, random 11.1 or above, or HbA1c 6.5 or above. Initial management is diet and exercise with home glucose monitoring; metformin or insulin is added if targets are not met after two weeks. Fasting target under 5.1 mmol/L and postprandial targets under 6.7 mmol/L at 2 hours are typical for AU maternity units.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 (any one).
Overt diabetes: fasting 7.0, random 11.1, HbA1c 6.5.
First line: diet, exercise, home glucose monitoring.
Add metformin or insulin at 2 weeks if targets missed.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS diagnosis of GDM requires only ONE abnormal OGTT value; a 1 hour of 10.4 mmol/L alone is enough even with normal fasting and 2 hour values.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM Testing in Australia

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 attends her 28-week antenatal appointment. Her blood group at booking was O rhesus D negative and her antibody screen was negative. Her partner is known to be rhesus D positive. She has had no vaginal bleeding, no antenatal invasive procedures, and no abdominal trauma this pregnancy.

She is asymptomatic today with a normal midwifery review. Fundal height and fetal heart tones are unremarkable. She asks about routine anti-D administration.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm at 28 weeks; longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation; fetal movements reported normal
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O rhesus D negative; antibody screen negative at 28 weeks; midstream urine and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D dosing schedule?

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscular now, one further dose at delivery
options.rationale: 250 IU is the correct dose for sensitising events in the first trimester, not for routine second and third trimester prophylaxis. (Source: NBA Anti-D guideline)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular at 34 weeks only, plus post-delivery dose
options.rationale: The NBA regimen requires 625 IU at both 28 and 34 weeks; a single-dose schedule at 34 weeks alone is inadequate. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular now and again at 34 weeks
options.rationale: NBA routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU at both 28 and 34 weeks gestation, plus a post-delivery dose within 72 hours if baby is Rh D positive. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU intramuscular now as a single-dose regimen
options.rationale: 1500 IU single-dose regimen is a UK NICE alternative; the AU NBA program uses two-dose 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: No anti-D required unless a sensitising event occurs before delivery
options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis reduces sensitisation from silent feto-maternal haemorrhage; withholding it fails Australian standard care. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: The National Blood Authority anti-D program in Australia gives 625 IU intramuscular at 28 and 34 weeks gestation to all non-sensitised rhesus D negative women, plus 625 IU within 72 hours of delivery if the baby is rhesus D positive. Sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, trauma) trigger extra dosing: 250 IU in first trimester, 625 IU from 13 weeks with Kleihauer testing to assess feto-maternal haemorrhage volume. Additional doses are calculated at 125 IU per mL of fetal red cells above the baseline detection.
key_points: AU regimen: 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks routinely.
Post-delivery: 625 IU within 72 hours if baby Rh D positive.
First trimester sensitising event: 250 IU.
13 weeks or later sensitising event: 625 IU with Kleihauer.
explanation.pearls: AU routine antenatal anti-D is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks; the 1500 IU single-dose regimen is UK NICE, not NBA.

sources.label: NBA: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 33 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of moderate painless bright red vaginal bleeding while at rest. Her previous births were two lower segment caesarean sections. Her 20-week morphology scan reported an anterior placenta reaching to the internal os.

She has soaked one large pad. Fetal movements have been active throughout. She has had no abdominal trauma, no contractions and no ruptured membranes. She last ate two hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min baseline with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Soft, non-tender abdomen; uterus relaxed between reassuring fetal movements; speculum deferred pending imaging
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and group and hold sent; CTG reactive with reassuring baseline; large-bore IV access secured

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next single step?

options.text: Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilation and any presenting cord
options.rationale: Digital examination is contraindicated in known or suspected placenta praevia before ultrasound has excluded a low-lying placenta at the os. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta and placenta praevia)

options.text: Speculum examination in lithotomy after gentle betadine cleaning of the vulva
options.rationale: Speculum examination is safe once praevia excluded but should not be the immediate next step before imaging in ongoing bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta and placenta praevia)

options.text: Immediate emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia in theatre
options.rationale: The mother is stable, fetus reassuring; category 1 caesarean is reserved for maternal or fetal compromise, not for painless bleeding at 33 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Kleihauer test only and outpatient follow-up given painless nature of bleed
options.rationale: Any antepartum haemorrhage at 33 weeks requires admission, imaging, fetal monitoring and steroids; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum haemorrhage)

options.text: Bedside transabdominal then transvaginal ultrasound to confirm placental position
options.rationale: Painless bleeding at 33 weeks with anterior low placenta and two prior caesareans mandates urgent ultrasound to confirm praevia or accreta before any vaginal examination. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Painless bright red bleeding at 33 weeks with a low anterior placenta and prior caesareans is placenta praevia (with placenta accreta risk) until proven otherwise. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated before imaging. Transabdominal then transvaginal ultrasound confirms placental position and screens for accreta features. Management includes admission, betamethasone for lung maturity from 22+0 to 34+6 weeks, tocolysis only if in threatened preterm labour, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if birth is anticipated within 24 hours, and elective caesarean section at 36 to 37 weeks if praevia persists.
key_points: Painless bright red APH implicates praevia over abruption.
Never examine digitally before ultrasound in suspected praevia.
Two prior caesareans plus anterior praevia raises accreta risk.
Betamethasone from 22+0 to 34+6 weeks reduces neonatal RDS.
explanation.pearls: For painless APH at 33 weeks with prior caesareans and low anterior placenta, get transvaginal ultrasound before any digital examination; accreta risk is high.

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 attends the first-trimester ultrasound at 12 weeks after a spontaneous conception. Imaging shows twin fetuses with a single placental mass, a thin dividing membrane and no evidence of a lambda sign at the base. She has no personal or family history of twinning and did not use fertility treatment.

Both fetuses are appropriately grown for gestation with crown-rump lengths within 5 percent of each other. She is asymptomatic and reports normal fetal movements at this early stage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rates 168 and 172/min
data_table.Examination: Uterus corresponding with 12 to 14 weeks gestation; abdomen otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 12 weeks; nuchal translucency 1.8 mm and 1.9 mm; combined first trimester screen result pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional antenatal surveillance schedule?

options.text: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for growth and amniotic fluid discordance
options.rationale: RANZCOG requires fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in MCDA twins to detect twin to twin transfusion syndrome and growth discordance early. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Four-weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks matching dichorionic diamniotic surveillance
options.rationale: Four-weekly ultrasound is appropriate for DCDA; MCDA needs fortnightly from 16 weeks because of TTTS risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Monthly maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein screening from 18 weeks to term
options.rationale: Serial AFP is not part of AU MCDA surveillance; the primary risk (TTTS) is detected on ultrasound, not biochemistry. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Weekly fetal heart auscultation from 24 weeks with routine standard ultrasound only
options.rationale: Weekly auscultation alone misses TTTS which is diagnosed by ultrasound; standard biometry frequency is inadequate for MCDA. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Weekly cardiotocography from 26 weeks with three-monthly growth scans thereafter
options.rationale: CTG has no role in early MCDA surveillance and three-monthly growth scans are too infrequent to detect TTTS. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Monochorionicity carries the twin to twin transfusion syndrome risk (10 to 15 percent), acute intertwin transfusion at delivery, and selective fetal growth restriction. RANZCOG mandates fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in MCDA pregnancies for amniotic fluid, fetal size and Doppler discordance. DCDA pregnancies are surveilled monthly. Timed delivery in uncomplicated MCDA is 36 to 37 weeks; DCDA is 37 to 38 weeks; monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) delivered 32 to 34 weeks under continuous inpatient monitoring.
key_points: MCDA: fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks (TTTS surveillance).
DCDA: monthly ultrasound from 20 weeks.
MCMA: continuous inpatient from 26 weeks with delivery 32 to 34 weeks.
Timed birth MCDA at 36 to 37 weeks.
explanation.pearls: MCDA twins get fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for TTTS; DCDA get monthly from 20 weeks; the T-sign versus lambda sign at 12 weeks determines the surveillance schedule.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is reviewed at her six-week postnatal check after her first birth. She scores 16 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale with a positive response to item 10 (thoughts of self-harm reported as fleeting, no plan, no intent). She is exclusively breastfeeding a well-thriving infant.

She describes anhedonia, poor sleep beyond that expected with a newborn, and reduced appetite. She has no prior psychiatric history, is not on any medications, and has strong partner and family supports. She is willing to consider medication and continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and cooperative; tearful when discussing infant care but engaged; no active psychosis; safety planning completed with partner
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 16; TSH 1.8 mIU/L (within normal limits); ferritin 42 mcg/L (within normal limits)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg oral daily with weekly review during initial titration phase
options.rationale: Paroxetine has short half-life and higher discontinuation symptoms; sertraline is preferred first-line in breastfeeding per COPE. (Source: COPE Perinatal Guideline)

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg oral daily with blood pressure monitoring in first month
options.rationale: Venlafaxine transfers into breastmilk more than SSRIs and has higher discontinuation risk; SSRI first-line preferred. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg oral nightly with weekly weight and sedation monitoring
options.rationale: Mirtazapine causes sedation and appetite change and carries less breastfeeding safety data than sertraline; not first-line here. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg oral daily with weekly review during initial titration phase
options.rationale: Sertraline is the AU first-line SSRI in breastfeeding due to lowest infant plasma concentrations and strongest safety data (COPE). (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg oral daily with monthly review for breastfeeding infant sedation
options.rationale: Fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine accumulate in the infant due to long half-lives; not first choice in breastfeeding. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

explanation.summary: COPE recommends sertraline as first-line SSRI in breastfeeding because relative infant dose is under 2 percent and infant plasma concentrations are consistently undetectable. Paroxetine is acceptable in pregnancy exposure continuation but not first-choice. Fluoxetine has active long half-life metabolite; venlafaxine transfers more. Sertraline is started at 50 mg with review at 1 to 2 weeks; response is expected at 4 to 6 weeks. Safety planning includes partner involvement, community mental health referral for EPDS above 12 with self-harm ideation, and infant sedation monitoring in the first two weeks.
key_points: Sertraline is first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (COPE).
EPDS 16 with self-harm ideation warrants safety planning and referral.
Fluoxetine's long half-life makes it less suitable in breastfeeding.
Sertraline titration: start 50 mg, review 1 to 2 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline 50 mg daily is the AU first-line SSRI in breastfeeding perinatal depression; relative infant dose is under 2 percent, unlike fluoxetine which accumulates.

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 is at 41 weeks gestation, in active second stage. The head delivers but the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with the next contraction and turtle-neck sign is present. Additional help has already been called. The registrar has coached her out of the pushing position and drained the bladder. McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure have been applied for one contraction cycle without progress.

Her estimated fetal weight was 4.4 kg. This is her second delivery; her first infant was 3.8 kg vaginally without complication. She has an epidural in situ. Time from head delivery is now 90 seconds and the fetal heart rate is 100/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, fetal heart rate 100/min
data_table.Examination: Head fully delivered, turtle-neck sign persistent; McRoberts in position, suprapubic pressure applied; perineum intact so far
data_table.Investigations: None applicable; ongoing intrapartum team present including senior obstetrician on the way; paediatric team in room

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement and immediate caesarean section
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last-resort option after all other manoeuvres have failed; not appropriate at 90 seconds having tried only McRoberts and SPP. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Enter the posterior vagina to deliver the posterior arm across the fetal chest
options.rationale: After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, RANZCOG HELPERR sequence proceeds to internal manoeuvres, of which delivery of the posterior arm has the highest success rate. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Apply strong axial traction to the fetal head with the mother in McRoberts
options.rationale: Excessive traction risks brachial plexus injury; when McRoberts fails the next step is internal manoeuvres, not more traction. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Perform symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to widen the pelvic outlet
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is not part of AU shoulder dystocia sequence; it is a last-resort resource-poor manoeuvre with high morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

options.text: Turn the mother onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) and re-attempt gentle traction only
options.rationale: Gaskin is an accepted variant but internal manoeuvres (posterior arm or Wood's screw) have higher success once external manoeuvres fail; posterior arm is highest yield. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG uses the HELPERR mnemonic for shoulder dystocia: call for Help, evaluate for Episiotomy, place in McRoberts (Legs), suprapubic Pressure, Enter for internal rotation (Wood's screw or Rubin manoeuvre), Remove posterior arm, Roll onto all fours. Once external manoeuvres (McRoberts plus SPP) fail after a single cycle, proceed immediately to internal manoeuvres; delivery of the posterior arm has the highest single-manoeuvre success rate. Time from head to body delivery beyond 5 minutes markedly increases hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy risk, so escalation must be prompt. Zavanelli cephalic replacement is reserved for failure of all HELPERR steps.
key_points: HELPERR sequence sits behind AU shoulder dystocia response.
Posterior arm delivery has highest single-manoeuvre success.
Avoid excessive axial traction (brachial plexus risk).
Zavanelli is last-resort, not early option.
explanation.pearls: When McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure fail for shoulder dystocia, deliver the posterior arm next; it has the highest success rate of internal manoeuvres per RANZCOG.

subtopic_detail: Abdominal pain three days after methotrexate for a tubal ectopic
stem: A 27-year-old woman treated with methotrexate three days ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy returns with lower abdominal pain that began this morning. She has not fainted and has no shoulder tip pain. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa without guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 116/74, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L, was 126 g/L; hCG 2,450 IU/L, day 0 was 2,200 IU/L
data_table.Ultrasound: Unchanged 20 mm right adnexal mass; small volume free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with repeat haemoglobin and hCG
options.rationale: Separation pain is common between days 2 and 7, and with stable observations, a stable haemoglobin and only a trace of free fluid, observation with serial testing distinguishes it from rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Transfer to theatre now for laparoscopic salpingectomy
options.rationale: Immediate surgery is for tachycardia or hypotension, a falling haemoglobin, peritonism or a large volume of free fluid, which would together indicate rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Give a second dose of methotrexate and discharge her home
options.rationale: The decision about a second dose is made on the day 4 to day 7 hCG change, and a rise at day 3 is the expected pattern rather than evidence of failure. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Discharge with oral analgesia and review in four days
options.rationale: Outpatient review suits settling pain in a woman who lives close to the hospital and has normal observations; new pain on the day it starts is safer assessed with serial haemoglobin. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
options.rationale: Computed tomography is used when an alternative surgical cause is suspected and ultrasound is unhelpful; transvaginal ultrasound answers the question here without irradiating the pelvis. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pain in the first week after methotrexate is common and usually reflects tubal abortion or distension as the trophoblast separates, which is why women are warned to expect it. Distinguishing separation pain from rupture rests on the observations, the haemoglobin trend, the volume of free fluid and the clinical examination, not on the pain itself or on the hCG, which typically rises to a peak around day 4. Stable parameters allow admission for observation with serial haemoglobin and hCG; any deterioration, significant free fluid or peritonism means theatre. In context, every woman given methotrexate should leave with written advice on what pain to expect, when to return, and where to present out of hours.
key_points: Separation pain typically occurs between days 2 and 7 after methotrexate.
A rising hCG at day 4 is expected and not evidence of failure.
Observations, haemoglobin trend and free fluid volume separate this from rupture.
Serial haemoglobin and hCG with inpatient observation is the safe middle course.
explanation.pearls: Shoulder tip pain, syncope or a falling haemoglobin turn expectant observation into an emergency, and neither the hCG level nor the size of the adnexal mass predicts rupture.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G3P2) is 20 minutes postpartum after an unassisted vaginal delivery of a 4.1 kg baby at 40+3 weeks. Blood loss is measured at 1200 mL and continuing. Her placenta was delivered intact with controlled cord traction and Syntocinon 10 units IM was given at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Her third-stage bleeding continued and she has already had a Syntocinon 40 unit infusion started.

On bimanual examination the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus. There is no visible perineal, vaginal or cervical laceration on inspection. Her booking bloods showed haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160) with normal platelets and coagulation profile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and 2 cm above the umbilicus; no perineal, vaginal or cervical laceration on speculum inspection; bladder empty via indwelling catheter
data_table.Investigations: Two large-bore IV lines in situ; crossmatch sent; venous blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and prepare for further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Ergometrine 250 micrograms IM is the RANZCOG second-line uterotonic when the uterus remains atonic on maximal oxytocin, provided blood pressure and cardiovascular history do not contraindicate it. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Repeat IM Syntocinon 10 units bolus with continued uterine massage
options.rationale: A second bolus of oxytocin adds little when a Syntocinon infusion is already running at ceiling and gives inadequate tone response for ongoing atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Intramyometrial carboprost 250 micrograms directly into the uterine fundus
options.rationale: Carboprost is a fourth-line uterotonic reserved for haemorrhage refractory to oxytocin and ergometrine and is generally IM, not intramyometrial at first pass. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 gram IV alone without any further uterotonic therapy
options.rationale: TXA is an adjunct that reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours but does not treat atony; uterotonic escalation is the primary tone-directed step. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Insert a Bakri balloon and defer any additional uterotonic administration
options.rationale: Mechanical tamponade is a step when pharmacological measures fail; RANZCOG advises exhausting uterotonics before balloon insertion. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Australian PPH management follows the four Ts framework and escalates uterotonics in a fixed pharmacological order. Oxytocin (IM bolus then infusion) is first; ergometrine 250 micrograms IM is second when tone remains poor; carboprost (Hemabate) 250 micrograms IM is third; misoprostol PR is a fourth or adjunct option. Tranexamic acid 1 gram IV is a mandatory adjunct within 3 hours regardless of the tone pathway. Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, Bakri balloon) sit alongside surgical escalation once pharmacological options are exhausted.
key_points: Oxytocin then ergometrine then carboprost is the RANZCOG uterotonic ladder.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and severe cardiac disease.
TXA 1 g IV is an adjunct, not a uterotonic substitute.
Bakri balloon follows failure of pharmacological measures.
explanation.pearls: When the uterus stays soft on maximal oxytocin, give ergometrine 250 micrograms IM next; hold it only if the blood pressure is above 140/90 or there is significant cardiac disease. TXA 1 gram IV runs concurrently in every PPH within 3 hours.

subtopic_detail: Plateauing hCG after conservative tubal surgery
stem: A 32-year-old woman had a laparoscopic salpingostomy two weeks ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy, chosen to preserve the tube. She is well, with no pain and normal observations, and attends for her weekly hCG result.

data_table.Serum hCG: Day 0: 1,900 IU/L; day 7: 420 IU/L; day 14: 380 IU/L
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L; creatinine 62 micromol/L; ALT 20 U/L
data_table.Ultrasound: No adnexal mass; empty uterus; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intramuscular methotrexate and continue weekly hCG
options.rationale: A plateau after salpingostomy indicates persistent trophoblast in the remaining tube, which occurs in up to one in ten and is treated medically when the woman is well and stable. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the hCG in four weeks with no other action
options.rationale: Simple surveillance is appropriate while the level is still falling steadily towards undetectable, not once it has plateaued with tubal tissue left in place. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy of that tube
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for bleeding, pain with haemodynamic change, or a plateau that persists after methotrexate, and it removes the tube the first operation was chosen to preserve. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange uterine curettage to exclude retained trophoblast
options.rationale: Curettage addresses an intrauterine pregnancy or retained products after miscarriage, and the uterus was empty on ultrasound at diagnosis and remains so. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Start a course of oral misoprostol over the next three days
options.rationale: Misoprostol is used for uterine evacuation and for postpartum haemorrhage; it has no effect on trophoblast persisting within the fallopian tube. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

explanation.summary: Salpingostomy leaves trophoblast behind in up to 10 per cent of cases, which is why hCG is followed to undetectable after conservative surgery and why salpingectomy is preferred when the other tube is healthy. Persistent trophoblast shows itself as a plateau or a rise after an initial fall, usually in a woman who feels well. A single dose of intramuscular methotrexate resolves most cases, with weekly hCG continuing until it is undetectable; surgery is kept for bleeding, pain or failure of the medical treatment. In context, any hCG that plateaus rather than falling after treatment of an ectopic pregnancy needs an explanation, and gestational trophoblastic disease belongs in the differential when the pattern is unusual.
key_points: Persistent trophoblast complicates up to one in ten salpingostomies.
Follow hCG weekly to undetectable after tube-conserving surgery.
A plateau or rise in a well woman is treated with methotrexate.
Salpingectomy is preferred when the contralateral tube is healthy.
explanation.pearls: The hCG pattern, not the symptoms, detects persistent trophoblast; most affected women feel entirely well at the visit where the plateau is found.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium and delivery timing
stem:
A 34-year-old primigravida is admitted at 34+2 weeks with a 24-hour history of frontal headache and epigastric discomfort. Her blood pressure at booking was 118/72. On arrival her blood pressure is 168/112 despite 20 mg oral nifedipine 30 minutes ago, then 154/98 after a second 20 mg dose. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and spot urine protein:creatinine is 82 mg/mmol.

She has +2 patellar hyperreflexia with no clonus. The fetus is active with a reactive CTG. She has no visual disturbance now and denies chest pain. She has had no antenatal steroids. Her husband is beside her and she has consented to admission and further investigations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 154/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15; +2 patellar reflexes bilaterally, no clonus; fundal height 34 cm; CTG reactive with baseline 145 and normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-450); ALT 78 U/L (<40); creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); LDH 340 U/L; spot urine protein:creatinine 82 mg/mmol (<30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM as a single dose and immediate caesarean section
options.rationale: Delivery is planned for this gestation but seizure prophylaxis is the immediate life-saving priority; a single steroid dose is inadequate for lung maturation. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Commence intravenous labetalol 20 mg boluses and titrate to a systolic under 140
options.rationale: Target BP in severe pre-eclampsia is systolic 130-150 and diastolic 80-100; overshooting below 130 systolic risks fetoplacental hypoperfusion. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Administer IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus followed by a 1 g/hour infusion
options.rationale: Severe hypertension with symptoms of impending eclampsia (headache, epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, HELLP-range labs) meets criteria for seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate per SOMANZ. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Sodium nitroprusside infusion for tighter blood pressure control and re-review
options.rationale: Nitroprusside is not first-line in pregnancy due to cyanide toxicity risk to the fetus; labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine are preferred. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Watchful monitoring on the antenatal ward with 4-hourly blood pressure charting
options.rationale: Symptomatic severe pre-eclampsia with laboratory evidence of end-organ involvement requires HDU-level monitoring and active treatment, not observation. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate is the first-line seizure prophylaxis for severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia per SOMANZ, given as a 4 gram IV loading dose over 15 to 20 minutes followed by a 1 gram per hour maintenance infusion for at least 24 hours (or 24 hours after last seizure). Signs of impending eclampsia include severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, clonus and HELLP-range biochemistry. Blood pressure targets in pregnancy are systolic 130-150 and diastolic 80-100 with labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine. Definitive treatment is delivery, timed after magnesium is established and BP controlled.
key_points: Magnesium is prophylactic; the load is 4 g IV over 15-20 min then 1 g/hour.
Target BP is 130-150 systolic; do not drop below 130.
Impending eclampsia signs: headache, RUQ pain, hyperreflexia, clonus.
Delivery follows magnesium and BP control, not the reverse.
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia with headache and hyperreflexia at 34 weeks, MgSO4 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour infusion starts before delivery planning; monitor patellar reflexes and respiratory rate for magnesium toxicity.

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks after a 75 gram OGTT showed a 1-hour value of 10.6 mmol/L. She has been on dietary and exercise therapy with a diabetes educator for 3 weeks and monitors capillary glucose fasting and 2 hours after each main meal.

She is now 29+3 weeks. Her recent 7-day glucose profile shows fasting values consistently 5.6-6.1 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial values 7.4-8.1 mmol/L after breakfast, with acceptable readings after other meals. She is compliant with the diet plan and has gained 4 kg since booking. Fetal growth ultrasound at 28 weeks showed an estimated fetal weight on the 62nd centile with normal liquor and Dopplers.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft; fundal height 30 cm; fetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Home glucose profile as above; HbA1c 5.6 percent (nondiabetic under 5.7); no ketonuria; renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her diabetes management?

options.text: Continue dietary and exercise therapy alone and repeat the profile after 2 weeks
options.rationale: Fasting glucose is above the ADIPS target of under 5.1 mmol/L on repeated measurements; deferring pharmacotherapy delays glycaemic control. (Source: ADIPS GDM guideline)

options.text: Immediate induction of labour at 30 weeks to end pregnancy and eliminate the risk
options.rationale: Delivery at 30 weeks is inappropriate for glycaemic indications alone; ADIPS supports term delivery once glycaemic control is achieved. (Source: ADIPS GDM guideline)

options.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 gram twice daily over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Metformin is a second-line oral option in Australia; ADIPS favours insulin first-line for fasting failure due to more reliable glycaemic effect and TGA labelling. (Source: ADIPS GDM guideline)

options.text: Commence isophane insulin 0.1 units/kg at bedtime and titrate to fasting target
options.rationale: Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia despite maximal dietary therapy is the primary indication for basal insulin; ADIPS supports isophane at bedtime as the first-line agent. (Source: ADIPS GDM guideline)

options.text: Rapid-acting insulin aspart at each meal only with no basal insulin cover
options.rationale: Prandial-only insulin does not address the fasting hyperglycaemia which is her dominant profile; a basal agent targets the fasting reading. (Source: ADIPS GDM guideline)

explanation.summary: Australian ADIPS glucose targets in gestational diabetes are fasting under 5.1 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L. Dietary and exercise therapy is trialled first for 1 to 2 weeks; pharmacotherapy is started if targets are not achieved. Insulin is the ADIPS preferred first-line agent, tailored to the failed target: basal isophane at bedtime for fasting hyperglycaemia, rapid-acting aspart or lispro before meals for postprandial hyperglycaemia. Metformin is a second-line oral option, particularly in women declining insulin or with major insulin resistance.
key_points: ADIPS targets are fasting <5.1 and 2 hour post-meal <6.7 mmol/L.
Basal isophane targets fasting; rapid-acting aspart targets postprandial.
Metformin is second-line, not first in AU practice.
Delivery timing for well-controlled GDM is 39-40 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Persistent fasting glucose above 5.1 mmol/L in GDM after 2 weeks of diet is the trigger for bedtime basal isophane; add rapid-acting aspart only when postprandial values also breach 6.7.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman (G2P1) is 34+0 weeks with placenta praevia identified on her routine morphology scan at 20 weeks. A follow-up transvaginal scan at 32 weeks confirmed the placental edge covers the internal cervical os. She has had two small self-limiting antepartum bleeds at 30 and 33 weeks, each settling within 12 hours without further intervention.

Her previous pregnancy was a term uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a 3.2 kg baby with no operative history. She is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen. She has no coagulopathy and no prior uterine surgery. She has completed her Anti-D course and had betamethasone at the time of the second bleed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, fundal height 34 cm; no active vaginal bleeding on speculum; cervix closed and long
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160); platelets 220 x10^9/L (150-450); blood group O positive antibody negative; group and hold current

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: External cephalic version at 37 weeks followed by trial of vaginal delivery at term
options.rationale: ECV addresses malpresentation and has no role in placenta praevia; the underlying obstruction still prevents safe vaginal delivery. (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia statement)

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and reassess placental position digitally at term
options.rationale: Placenta praevia is an absolute contraindication to digital cervical examination and to attempted vaginal delivery due to catastrophic haemorrhage risk. (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia statement)

options.text: Immediate caesarean section today under regional anaesthesia in the operating theatre
options.rationale: There is no current bleeding or fetal compromise; elective delivery at 36-37 weeks reduces neonatal morbidity compared with delivery at 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia statement)

options.text: Planned induction of labour at 39 weeks with epidural once cervix is favourable for use
options.rationale: Induction and labour are contraindicated with placenta covering the os; the placenta obstructs the cervical canal and induction guarantees bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia statement)

options.text: Planned elective caesarean section at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks with group-specific blood available
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends planned caesarean at 36-37 weeks for placenta praevia, particularly with prior bleeding, to reduce the risk of unscheduled bleeding and emergency delivery. (Source: RANZCOG placenta praevia statement)

explanation.summary: For confirmed placenta praevia (placental edge covering the internal os on transvaginal ultrasound after 32 weeks), planned elective caesarean section is the standard AU approach. Timing is 36+0 to 37+0 weeks for women with prior antepartum haemorrhage and 37+0 to 38+0 weeks for asymptomatic women, per RANZCOG. Anti-D prophylaxis and antenatal steroids are given at the time of any bleed. Digital cervical examination and attempted vaginal delivery are contraindicated. Group-specific blood must be available, and a consultant obstetrician and anaesthetist should be present.
key_points: Planned caesarean 36-37 weeks with prior bleeding; 37-38 without.
Digital cervical exam is absolutely contraindicated.
Blood must be available on standby (typed and crossmatched).
Placenta accreta spectrum needs specific workup if prior CS present.
explanation.pearls: Placenta praevia with prior antepartum bleeding delivers by planned caesarean at 36-37 weeks; earlier delivery only if bleeding recurs and cannot be stabilised.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends for routine cervical screening. She has been screened regularly since age 25, with the last screen 5 years ago negative for HPV. She has no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no postcoital bleeding and no intermenstrual bleeding. She is on a combined oral contraceptive and has never been pregnant. She is fully vaccinated with Gardasil 9.

Her cervical screening test today returns HPV positive for non-16/18 oncogenic HPV. Reflex liquid-based cytology on the same sample is reported as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is well and works as a schoolteacher. She has no immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft; speculum shows a healthy pink cervix with no lesion or contact bleeding; bimanual exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test: HPV positive (non 16/18); reflex LBC: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 12 months to reassess HPV status and cytology together
options.rationale: Under the NCSP an HPV non 16/18 positive with negative LBC is intermediate risk; the algorithm directs a repeat test at 12 months. (Source: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Immediate colposcopic referral for directed biopsy of any abnormal transformation zone
options.rationale: Colposcopy is not indicated for HPV non 16/18 positive with negative cytology on first detection under the NCSP algorithm; repeat testing in 12 months is the pathway. (Source: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Return to routine 5-year screening as she has previously screened negative for HPV
options.rationale: A single HPV non 16/18 result cannot be dismissed; the intermediate-risk group requires 12-monthly repeat to detect persistence. (Source: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Refer to gynaecology for large loop excision of the transformation zone as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Excisional treatment without histological confirmation of high grade disease is inappropriate and risks preterm birth in future pregnancies. (Source: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.text: Test of cure by cervical smear alone in 6 months regardless of the HPV subtype result
options.rationale: There is no completed treatment to a test of cure would follow; the NCSP algorithm sits her in the intermediate-risk 12-month repeat category. (Source: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: Under the Australian National Cervical Screening Program, primary HPV testing every 5 years replaced the 2-yearly Pap smear in December 2017. If HPV 16 or 18 is detected, the woman is directly referred for colposcopy. If a non 16/18 oncogenic HPV type is detected, reflex LBC on the same sample is used: high-grade abnormality goes to colposcopy; low-grade or negative cytology sits in the intermediate-risk group with a repeat test at 12 months. Two consecutive HPV positives at 12-month interval refer to colposcopy regardless of cytology.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 positive: direct to colposcopy regardless of cytology.
HPV non 16/18 with normal or low-grade cytology: repeat at 12 months.
Two consecutive HPV positives refer to colposcopy.
Any high-grade cytology on reflex LBC refers to colposcopy.
explanation.pearls: HPV non 16/18 with negative cytology returns for repeat HPV in 12 months; two consecutive positives at 12-month interval then refer for colposcopy even if cytology stays negative.

sources.label: NCSP: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 weeks of intermittent light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 years ago. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and takes no other regular medications. She is otherwise well, BMI 27 kg/m2, has never been pregnant, and has no family history of endometrial or ovarian cancer.

You perform a transvaginal ultrasound in the same visit which shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a heterogeneous appearance. Both ovaries are quiescent and there is no free fluid. She has no personal history of breast cancer and has never used tamoxifen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass; speculum shows a small amount of old blood in the posterior fornix and a smooth pink cervix; bimanual exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 6 mm, heterogeneous; ovaries normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to observe any endometrial change over time
options.rationale: Ultrasound alone cannot exclude endometrial cancer once bleeding has occurred and endometrium is above 4 mm; histology is required. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Pipelle endometrial biopsy in the outpatient clinic for histological assessment now
options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness above 4 mm on TVS is an indication for endometrial sampling per RANZCOG; Pipelle is the first-line office biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Colposcopy with directed cervical biopsy of any acetowhite areas visualised
options.rationale: Colposcopy assesses cervical disease; the bleeding source here is more likely endometrial and requires endometrial sampling. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Serum CA125 measurement and CT abdomen/pelvis before any tissue diagnosis is sought
options.rationale: CA125 has poor specificity in postmenopausal bleeding and CT is not first-line for endometrial pathology; direct histology is the diagnostic step. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

options.text: Empirical continuous progestogen without any histological sampling of the endometrium
options.rationale: Treating without diagnosis is unsafe; a proportion of PMB cases represent endometrial carcinoma and require histology first. (Source: RANZCOG PMB statement)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding requires exclusion of endometrial carcinoma. RANZCOG uses transvaginal ultrasound as the first-line investigation; endometrial thickness under 4 mm has a very high negative predictive value for carcinoma in a non-tamoxifen user and often needs no further tissue sampling. Thickness of 4 mm or above, heterogeneous appearance, or persistent bleeding despite thin endometrium mandates endometrial biopsy. Pipelle is the outpatient standard; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy follows a failed Pipelle or persistent symptoms with negative sampling. Tamoxifen users get lower ultrasound utility and often go directly to hysteroscopic assessment.
key_points: Endometrial thickness cut-off is 4 mm on TVS for PMB in non tamoxifen users.
Above 4 mm needs Pipelle endometrial biopsy first-line.
Persistent bleeding with thin endometrium still needs hysteroscopy.
Tamoxifen users have reduced TVS utility.
explanation.pearls: In postmenopausal bleeding, an endometrial thickness above 4 mm on TVS mandates Pipelle biopsy in clinic; hysteroscopy follows if Pipelle fails or bleeding persists despite negative histology.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman presents seeking contraception. Her cycles were regular until 12 months ago and are now irregular with heavy bleeding and occasional hot flushes. She has 3 children by uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2, blood pressure is 148/92 on two readings, and she smokes 8 cigarettes a day. She has no personal history of VTE, breast cancer or migraine.

She does not wish to become pregnant, but she is bothered by menstrual heaviness (soaking a pad every 2 hours on the heaviest days) and mild vasomotor symptoms. She has not tried any hormonal method for 20 years. Her partner has had a vasectomy but they have separated and she has a new partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg (repeated), respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m2; abdomen soft with no mass; bimanual pelvic exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-160); ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-160); TSH within normal limits; urine bhCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol 30 microgram and levonorgestrel
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in a woman over 35 who smokes because of unacceptable cardiovascular and VTE risk. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection every 12 weeks
options.rationale: DMPA is progestogen-only and safe from a VTE standpoint, but reduces bone mineral density and is less useful for menorrhagia in perimenopause. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system for both contraception and heavy bleeding control
options.rationale: The LNG-IUS provides highly effective contraception, treats heavy menstrual bleeding, and is safe in smokers and those with hypertension; it also acts as endometrial protection if MHT is later added. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Vaginal ring containing ethinylestradiol and etonogestrel replaced every 21 days monthly
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception delivered vaginally still carries the same cardiovascular contraindications in a smoker over 35. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

options.text: Copper intrauterine device inserted at the earliest opportunity in your consulting rooms
options.rationale: The copper IUD is contraceptive but often worsens heavy menstrual bleeding, which is her primary presenting symptom; a hormonal option is preferred. (Source: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception)
source_refs: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

explanation.summary: In a smoker over 35 with hypertension, combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) due to cardiovascular and VTE hazard. Progestogen-only options are safe: the LNG-IUS is first-line when heavy menstrual bleeding coexists, giving 96 percent PBAC reduction and lasting 8 years for both contraception and treatment. DMPA reduces BMD and is less useful for menorrhagia. Copper IUD frequently worsens flow. The LNG-IUS also provides endometrial protection if oestrogen-based MHT is later added for vasomotor symptoms.
key_points: CHC is contraindicated in a smoker over 35 (UKMEC 4).
LNG-IUS combines contraception and menorrhagia treatment.
DMPA reduces bone density with long-term use.
Copper IUD often worsens heavy menstrual bleeding.
explanation.pearls: In perimenopausal smokers with hypertension and heavy periods, the 52 mg LNG-IUS is first choice: contraception, PBAC reduction, and future endometrial protection for MHT in one device.

sources.label: FSRH UK MEC / Australian eTG - Contraception

subtopic_detail: Suspected ovarian torsion imaging and management
stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 4 hours of sudden onset severe right lower quadrant pain associated with two episodes of vomiting. She reports intermittent similar but milder pain over the past 2 weeks that self-resolved within an hour. She is sexually active with a male partner using condoms; her last menstrual period was 10 days ago and was normal.

On examination she is uncomfortable and tender in the right adnexa without peritonism. A urinary bhCG is negative. Bedside ultrasound in ED shows an enlarged right ovary of 7.2 cm with peripherally displaced follicles and reduced arterial and venous Doppler flow compared with the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen tender in right iliac fossa and right adnexa without peritonism or guarding; cervix closed on speculum; no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinary bhCG negative; WCC 12.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 14 mg/L (<5); TVS: right ovary 7.2 cm with peripheral follicles and reduced Doppler flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for analgesia and observation with a repeat ultrasound in 12 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Delay increases the risk of irreversible ischaemic ovarian loss; suspected torsion is a surgical emergency and imaging findings already support the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline for empirical pelvic inflammatory disease cover
options.rationale: PID typically features vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness or fever; her picture and imaging fit torsion, and antibiotics do not treat the underlying vascular compromise. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to characterise the adnexal mass further
options.rationale: CT delays theatre without adding to the surgical decision; TVS with Doppler is the imaging modality of choice and is already suggestive. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy and detorsion with ovarian preservation as the primary aim
options.rationale: Clinical picture plus imaging supports adnexal torsion; laparoscopic detorsion within 6 hours preserves ovarian function even if the ovary appears dusky at surgery. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

options.text: Oophorectomy at open laparotomy without initial attempt at conservative detorsion
options.rationale: Oophorectomy at the first look loses fertility unnecessarily; RANZCOG supports laparoscopic detorsion first even in a dusky ovary. (Source: RANZCOG adnexal mass statement)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency in women of reproductive age. The classical picture is sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain often with vomiting, sometimes preceded by intermittent pain from partial torsion. TVS with Doppler shows an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles and reduced or absent flow; presence of Doppler flow does not exclude torsion. Definitive management is laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation, even if the ovary appears blue-black at surgery, because recovery of function is common. Oophorectomy is reserved for necrosis or when malignancy is suspected.
key_points: TVS with Doppler is first-line imaging; flow presence does not exclude torsion.
Detorsion within 6 hours preserves ovarian function.
Oophorectomy is reserved for necrosis or malignancy.
Cystectomy of any cyst is performed at the same laparoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an enlarged 7 cm ovary and reduced Doppler flow warrants urgent laparoscopy for detorsion; even a dusky ovary should be preserved rather than removed at first look.

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida is admitted to the day assessment unit at 9+2 weeks with a 3-week history of vomiting more than 8 times daily. She is unable to keep down oral fluids and has lost 4.5 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg (7 percent loss). Urine dipstick is positive for ketones 4+ and specific gravity is 1.030. Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L.

She has already been prescribed pyridoxine 25 mg TDS and metoclopramide 10 mg TDS in the community for 5 days without benefit. She is not on any other medication. Thyroid function is within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound this morning shows a viable singleton with cardiac activity present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick ketones 4+, specific gravity 1.030; sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-7.0); TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition via peripherally inserted central catheter for 2 weeks now
options.rationale: TPN carries VTE, infection and metabolic risks and is a last-line intervention; IV rehydration and antiemetic escalation come first. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Increase metoclopramide to 20 mg oral four times daily and reassess in 48 hours at home
options.rationale: Doubling an already-failed oral antiemetic in a woman who cannot tolerate oral fluids does not address ongoing ketonuria and hypokalaemia. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily as first-line escalation for symptom control
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of standard antiemetics including ondansetron; they are not first-line escalation. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Consider medical termination of pregnancy at 9 weeks to end the underlying trigger
options.rationale: Termination is not an initial management step in refractory nausea; stepwise pharmacological escalation is required first and most women improve into the second trimester. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

options.text: Admit for IV fluid resuscitation, ondansetron 4 mg IV 8 hourly and thiamine cover
options.rationale: She has failed first-line pyridoxine plus metoclopramide with ketonuria and 7 percent weight loss; admission for IV rehydration, ondansetron and thiamine matches the RANZCOG stepwise algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG hyperemesis statement)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by persistent vomiting with weight loss over 5 percent, dehydration and ketonuria. First-line is pyridoxine (25 mg 8-hourly) with or without doxylamine. Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or ondansetron are added if symptoms persist; ondansetron is not associated with a meaningful teratogenic signal per contemporary data but is generally reserved for second-line after first-line failure. Refractory disease with electrolyte disturbance requires admission for IV fluids, thiamine and IV antiemetics; corticosteroids or TPN are last-line options.
key_points: First-line: pyridoxine +/- doxylamine.
Second-line: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or ondansetron.
Admission if 5 percent weight loss, ketonuria or failed oral therapy.
Thiamine cover before IV dextrose to prevent Wernicke.
explanation.pearls: HG that has failed pyridoxine + metoclopramide with ketonuria and 7 percent weight loss needs admission for IV Hartmann's plus ondansetron plus thiamine; steroids come only if IV antiemetics fail.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman (G3P2) attends the antenatal clinic at 34 weeks to discuss her mode of delivery. Her first delivery was an emergency lower segment caesarean section for fetal distress at 8 cm dilatation at term. Her second delivery was an uncomplicated elective repeat lower segment caesarean at 39 weeks. She now wishes to attempt a vaginal birth after caesarean.

Her operative notes describe a low transverse uterine incision at both prior surgeries with no extension. She has a healthy singleton fetus in cephalic presentation, estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, and adequate liquor. She has no other maternal medical problems. This antenatal clinic uses continuous intrapartum fetal monitoring and can offer immediate caesarean recovery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 138/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 34 cm; fetus cephalic; abdomen soft; scar Pfannenstiel well-healed
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 32 weeks: cephalic, EFW 55th centile, normal liquor; previous operative notes: two low transverse incisions without extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Offer planned VBAC with continuous CTG monitoring in labour and one-to-one midwifery care
options.rationale: With two low transverse caesareans, a stable current pregnancy, cephalic presentation and no other contraindications, VBAC can be offered with informed consent, continuous CTG and immediate access to caesarean recovery. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Two prior caesareans is an absolute contraindication and mandates elective caesarean now
options.rationale: Two prior low transverse caesareans is not an absolute contraindication in RANZCOG guidance; VBAC after two caesareans can be considered with informed counselling. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and titrated oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction in a woman with a scarred uterus is associated with substantially increased rupture risk and is generally avoided. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Recommend home birth given her strong preference for a vaginal birth in this pregnancy
options.rationale: Prior caesarean is a contraindication to planned home birth in Australia because emergency caesarean access is essential for scar rupture management. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

options.text: Arrange elective classical uterine incision caesarean at 37 weeks for safer scar assessment
options.rationale: A classical (vertical) incision is not indicated when previous incisions were low transverse and carries much higher rupture risk in future pregnancies. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC statement)

explanation.summary: Planned VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean) can be offered after one or two prior low transverse caesareans with informed consent, continuous CTG monitoring in labour, and access to immediate caesarean recovery. Absolute contraindications include prior classical or T-shaped uterine incision, prior uterine rupture, and some contraindications to any vaginal delivery (major placenta praevia, transverse lie unrelieved). Induction with prostaglandins is discouraged due to scar rupture risk; mechanical methods (Foley) or oxytocin alone are preferred. Success rates approach 70 percent overall and 90 percent when a previous vaginal birth occurred.
key_points: One or two prior low transverse caesareans is not an absolute contraindication.
Classical or T-shaped incision is an absolute contraindication.
Prostaglandin induction carries increased rupture risk on a scarred uterus.
Home birth is contraindicated after prior caesarean.
explanation.pearls: Two prior low transverse caesareans with a well-positioned cephalic fetus is a legitimate VBAC candidate in Australia, with counselling, continuous CTG and prompt caesarean access; avoid prostaglandin induction.
