subtopic_detail: Antibiotic plan when membranes rupture preterm in a known carrier
stem: A 27-year-old woman attends at 31 weeks after a gush of clear fluid two hours ago. She is not contracting and the first dose of betamethasone has been given.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 30 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Findings: Pooled clear liquor, cervix closed, temperature 36.7 degC, normal cardiotocograph

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral erythromycin for ten days, with the penicillin held until labour
options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs latency after preterm rupture, while the intrapartum penicillin is timed to labour or planned birth. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin four hourly from now until the baby is born
options.rationale: Continuous penicillin from rupture would be right if she were labouring or birth were being expedited today. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.text: Oral erythromycin for ten days together with penicillin four hourly
options.rationale: Running both is appropriate once labour establishes, not during expectant management that may last weeks. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin, with birth expedited this evening
options.rationale: That combination and immediate birth belong to suspected intrauterine infection, signalled by fever or fetal tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
Australian Medicines Handbook - benzylpenicillin and vancomycin

options.text: No antibiotic, with twice daily observations while awaiting spontaneous labour
options.rationale: Withholding latency antibiotics would shorten the time gained for corticosteroids to work and raises infection rates. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth

explanation.summary: Two separate antibiotic decisions sit on top of each other after preterm prelabour rupture of the membranes in a colonised woman, and the reasoning is to keep them apart. The first is latency: a ten day course of erythromycin after rupture prolongs pregnancy, reduces neonatal infection and buys time for corticosteroids, and it begins now. The second is intrapartum prophylaxis against group B streptococcus, which is timed to established labour or to a planned birth because its benefit depends on concentrations at the moment of exposure; running it for the whole latency period selects resistant organisms without adding protection. Co-amoxiclav is avoided in this setting because of an association with necrotising enterocolitis. In context, expectant management continues with surveillance for intrauterine infection, and any fever, uterine tenderness or fetal tachycardia changes the plan to broad-spectrum treatment and birth.
key_points: Latency erythromycin for ten days starts at the time of preterm rupture.
Intrapartum prophylaxis is timed to established labour or planned birth.
Co-amoxiclav is avoided because of necrotising enterocolitis risk.
Fever, uterine tenderness or fetal tachycardia shifts management to broad-spectrum cover and birth.
explanation.pearls: Antenatal corticosteroids and, below 30 weeks, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection run alongside the antibiotic plan, and the whole point of latency treatment is to let those interventions take effect.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G1P1) presents to the emergency department on day 4 postpartum after a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a manual removal of retained placental tissue at the time of delivery. She reports 24 hours of fever, offensive-smelling vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain. She is exclusively breastfeeding without any breast concerns.

On examination the fundus is 4 finger-breadths above the symphysis pubis and boggy, with cervical excitation and marked lower abdominal tenderness. She has no signs of skin infection at the perineum. She has no known drug allergies. She has not received antibiotics since delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender, boggy, 4 fingerbreadths above symphysis; offensive lochia; cervical excitation; no perineal skin infection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.1 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 168 mg/L (<5); lactate 3.2 mmol/L; blood cultures taken; endocervical swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone until formal culture sensitivity is available
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positives only and misses Gram negatives and anaerobes that dominate polymicrobial endometritis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days from ED discharge home
options.rationale: Sepsis with SIRS features and lactate above 2 requires IV therapy and admission; oral outpatient management is inadequate. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV amoxicillin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg all 8-hourly
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole is the standard Australian empirical regimen for severe puerperal sepsis, covering group A strep, Gram negatives and anaerobes. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy as broad Gram negative and Gram positive cover
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks reliable anaerobic cover which is essential in polymicrobial puerperal sepsis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

options.text: IV clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly with intravenous fluids only as first-line therapy today
options.rationale: Clindamycin alone lacks adequate Gram negative cover; a triple regimen or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Puerperal sepsis)

explanation.summary: Puerperal sepsis is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide. Empirical therapy must cover Group A streptococcus, Gram negatives (including E coli), Gram positives and anaerobes; Australian eTG recommends IV amoxicillin (or benzylpenicillin) plus gentamicin plus metronidazole for severe endometritis and puerperal sepsis. Retained products of conception require evacuation once the patient is stable on antibiotics. Early sepsis recognition using SIRS or qSOFA, source control and hour-1 IV antibiotics are critical.
key_points: Standard triple: amoxicillin/benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole.
Antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition.
Look for and evacuate retained products.
Group A streptococcus can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum sepsis with boggy uterus and offensive lochia after a manual removal needs triple IV amoxicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole within the sepsis hour bundle, then imaging for retained products.

stem:
A 26-year-old primigravida with known type 1 von Willebrand disease is reviewed at 34 weeks in the combined obstetric-haematology clinic. Her sister has the same diagnosis. She has a history of heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and prolonged bleeding after wisdom tooth extraction that responded to tranexamic acid and desmopressin.

Her third trimester coagulation screen today shows von Willebrand factor:antigen 92 IU/dL (50-150), von Willebrand factor:ristocetin cofactor activity 88 IU/dL (50-150), factor VIII activity 110 IU/dL (50-150). She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy so far. Baseline haemoglobin is 120 g/L and platelets are 240 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundal height 34 cm, no bruising, no petechiae, no active bleeding
data_table.Investigations: VWF:Ag 92 IU/dL, VWF:RCo 88 IU/dL, FVIII 110 IU/dL; Hb 120 g/L; platelets 240 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 4.8 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Recommend termination of pregnancy given the significant peripartum bleeding risk exists
options.rationale: There is no clinical indication for termination in a well-controlled type 1 vWD pregnancy with autocorrected factor levels. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 38 weeks under general anaesthesia to avoid regional block
options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated on haematological grounds when VWF activity is above 50; regional anaesthesia is acceptable at these levels. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Prophylactic von Willebrand factor concentrate infusion at onset of established labour
options.rationale: VWF concentrate is reserved for VWF activity under 50 IU/dL at delivery or type 2 or 3 disease; her third trimester levels have autocorrected. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery with active third stage and prophylactic tranexamic acid at delivery
options.rationale: Type 1 vWD with third trimester VWF activity above 50 IU/dL can deliver vaginally with active third stage and prophylactic TXA, without requiring VWF concentrate. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

options.text: Avoid all regional anaesthesia in labour due to unacceptable haematoma risk in this patient
options.rationale: Regional anaesthesia is safe when VWF and FVIII activity are above 50 IU/dL; blanket avoidance denies effective analgesia. (Source: HSANZ vWD in pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand factor and factor VIII levels rise physiologically in pregnancy and often reach normal levels in type 1 vWD by the third trimester. Peripartum planning is based on VWF:RCo and FVIII activity at 34-36 weeks: above 50 IU/dL allows vaginal delivery, active third stage, and regional anaesthesia without VWF concentrate; below 50 requires DDAVP (if responsive and outside pre-eclampsia risk) or VWF concentrate at the onset of labour. Tranexamic acid can be given prophylactically for 5-7 days postpartum to reduce secondary PPH risk. Types 2 and 3 vWD, and any active bleeding, need haematologist-led planning.
key_points: VWF and FVIII rise in pregnancy; check at 34-36 weeks.
Levels above 50 IU/dL allow vaginal delivery and regional block.
TXA reduces secondary PPH in vWD.
DDAVP is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia risk.
explanation.pearls: Type 1 vWD with third trimester VWF:RCo and FVIII both above 50 IU/dL delivers vaginally with active third stage and prophylactic TXA; VWF concentrate is only needed if activity remains below 50.

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida presents at 29+3 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid per vagina and a steady leak since. Sterile speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix. There are no contractions on the tocograph, the CTG is reactive and there is no vaginal bleeding or foul discharge.

She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Her white cell count is normal and CRP is unremarkable. A high vaginal swab is sent for microscopy and culture; group B streptococcus status is currently unknown. She has no known drug allergies. She has completed her first dose of betamethasone in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, cervix long and closed; no active bleeding; abdomen soft, non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 5 mg/L (<5); high vaginal swab sent; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate latency antibiotic regimen?

options.text: No antibiotics unless the patient develops fever or fetal tachycardia during the admission
options.rationale: Withholding latency antibiotics ignores the ORACLE I benefit of shorter time to delivery and lower neonatal morbidity in PPROM. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days from ED admission today
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk in the ORACLE I trial. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours until membrane rupture reaches 24 hours in duration
options.rationale: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (not latency antibiotics) is warranted with penicillin at delivery; oral erythromycin is the latency regimen. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days for anaerobic cover of the genital tract
options.rationale: Metronidazole monotherapy does not prolong pregnancy in PPROM and is not first-line for latency; erythromycin is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

options.text: Oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days or until delivery
options.rationale: Erythromycin latency antibiotics per ORACLE I are the AU standard for PPROM to prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to NEC risk. (Source: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

explanation.summary: For preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) before 34 weeks, the aim is expectant management with corticosteroids (24-34+6 weeks), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection under 30 weeks, and latency antibiotics. RANZCOG endorses oral erythromycin 250 mg 4 times daily for 10 days (or until delivery) based on the ORACLE I trial - prolongs pregnancy, reduces chorioamnionitis and reduces neonatal morbidity. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to increased NEC risk. GBS-positive women receive intrapartum penicillin as well. Delivery is planned by 37 weeks or earlier for infection, fetal compromise or maternal indication.
key_points: Erythromycin latency antibiotics are the ORACLE I standard.
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to increased NEC risk.
Steroids 24-34+6 weeks and magnesium under 30 weeks.
Deliver by 37 weeks or earlier if complications arise.
explanation.pearls: PPROM before 34 weeks: oral erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days (or until delivery), corticosteroids, magnesium under 30 weeks; avoid amoxicillin with clavulanic acid due to NEC signal.

sources.label: RANZCOG preterm labour and birth statement

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida presents at 32+4 weeks with 6 hours of steady right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. Her booking blood pressure was 110/68 and today it is 138/86, then 132/82 on repeat 15 minutes later. She has no visual disturbance, headache or peripheral oedema. Urine dipstick shows trace protein and spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 24 mg/mmol.

The obstetric registrar wondered aloud about biliary colic and requested an abdominal ultrasound which showed a normal gallbladder without stones and an unremarkable liver. Her platelet count 4 weeks ago was 245 x10^9/L. She has had no PV bleeding and the CTG is reactive. She feels fetal movements normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, no papilloedema, no clonus, mild RUQ tenderness without guarding, no peripheral oedema; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); ALT 210 U/L (<40); AST 240 U/L (<40); LDH 620 U/L (<250); haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L; spot urine PCR 24 mg/mmol; blood film with schistocytes; INR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis driving your management plan?

options.text: HELLP syndrome with delivery planned once corticosteroids are commenced and BP controlled
options.rationale: Platelets under 100, LDH raised with low haptoglobin and schistocytes plus AST/ALT above 70 meets Tennessee HELLP criteria even without severe hypertension or heavy proteinuria; delivery is the definitive treatment. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with plans for immediate broad hepatic support and delivery
options.rationale: AFLP typically shows hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy with markedly raised INR and normal platelets initially; her INR is normal and haemolysis features fit HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Symptomatic gallstone pancreatitis given RUQ pain and elevated liver enzymes on presentation
options.rationale: Gallbladder is normal and lipase was not raised; thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis fit HELLP rather than pancreatitis. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Isolated pregnancy-related idiopathic thrombocytopenia (gestational) with likely spontaneous resolution
options.rationale: Gestational thrombocytopenia rarely drops below 100 and does not cause haemolysis or transaminitis; her biochemistry fits HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

options.text: Viral hepatitis with expectant management and monitoring of fetal wellbeing over the next week
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis presents with much higher ALT/AST (thousands), positive viral serology and no MAHA; the picture is HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ HDP guideline)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a variant of pre-eclampsia defined by haemolysis (LDH raised, haptoglobin low, schistocytes on blood film), elevated liver enzymes (AST or ALT over 70) and low platelets (under 100 x10^9/L). Up to 15 to 20 percent of HELLP cases occur without severe hypertension or proteinuria; failure to recognise this atypical presentation delays delivery. Definitive management is expedited delivery once maternal stabilised: corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation before 34 weeks, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and blood product support (platelets under 50 for caesarean, under 20 for vaginal delivery). Watch for subcapsular liver haematoma and DIC as complications.
key_points: Tennessee HELLP: platelets <100, LDH >600 or haemolysis, AST/ALT >70.
Up to 20 percent of HELLP has minimal hypertension or proteinuria.
Delivery is definitive treatment; steroids for lung maturity.
Complications include DIC and subcapsular liver haematoma.
explanation.pearls: New RUQ pain in the third trimester with platelets 82, LDH 620 and AST 240 is HELLP even at BP 132/82; give steroids, magnesium and plan delivery within 48 hours.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 months of vague abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has no vaginal bleeding, no bowel disturbance and no urinary symptoms. Her last menstrual period was 12 years ago. Her mother had breast cancer at age 71 and her paternal aunt had ovarian cancer at age 58. She has no BRCA testing.

You arrange a pelvic ultrasound which shows a 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 solid nodular papillary projections greater than 3 mm, thick internal septations and moderate colour flow. There is no free fluid and the right ovary is atrophic. Serum CA125 is 88 kU/L, serum HE4 elevated, and calculated risk of malignancy index (RMI) is 528.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild lower abdominal fullness, no ascites, no palpable mass; bimanual exam confirms left adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TVS: 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 papillary projections and thick septations; CA125 88 kU/L (<35); HE4 raised; RMI 528; family history as above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 3 months to observe any change in the mass or serum CA125 rise
options.rationale: Interval observation of a complex postmenopausal mass with RMI over 200 delays definitive diagnosis of malignancy and worsens survival. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgical staging as the primary management
options.rationale: RMI over 200 with complex ultrasound morphology and family history mandates referral to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary service, not to a general gynaecologist. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Referral to a general gynaecologist for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy on the next list
options.rationale: Laparoscopic cystectomy risks intraoperative rupture and upstaging in an RMI 528 mass; specialist oncology referral is required. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Percutaneous ultrasound guided biopsy of the adnexal mass by an interventional radiologist
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a suspicious ovarian mass risks intraperitoneal seeding and upstaging; primary surgical staging is preferred. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

options.text: Empirical neoadjuvant carboplatin plus paclitaxel chemotherapy before any surgical intervention
options.rationale: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a valid pathway for high-volume disease but must be initiated by gynaecological oncology after histological confirmation. (Source: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

explanation.summary: The Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology score (multilocular, solid areas, bilaterality, ascites, intra-abdominal metastases) and CA125 to triage adnexal masses. RMI over 200 identifies high risk of ovarian cancer and warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for primary surgical staging, ideally by a subspecialist. Percutaneous biopsy risks upstaging via seeding and is avoided when primary surgery is feasible. Family history strengthens the case for genetic counselling and BRCA testing. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may replace primary debulking in selected high-volume disease after histological confirmation.
key_points: RMI over 200 refers to a gynae oncology centre.
Percutaneous biopsy risks seeding; avoid when primary surgery feasible.
Genetic counselling for a strong family history.
Postmenopausal complex mass is malignancy until proven otherwise.
explanation.pearls: RMI 528 in a postmenopausal woman with papillary projections needs direct gynae-oncology referral for primary staging surgery; do not biopsy percutaneously and do not defer for interval imaging.

sources.label: eviQ Cancer Council: Ovarian cancer referral

stem:
A 31-year-old woman (G2P1) presents to your general practice at 25 weeks gestation for a routine antenatal review. She had a spontaneous conception, is on pregnancy multivitamins and iodine only, and has no diabetes symptoms. Her BMI at booking was 28 kg/m2. Her previous pregnancy was 3 years ago with an uneventful vaginal delivery at 39 weeks of a 3.4 kg baby and no documented GDM. She has no first-degree family history of diabetes.

A routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed today for universal screening returns fasting glucose 5.5 mmol/L, 1 hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L and 2 hour glucose 8.4 mmol/L. She has no symptoms of hyperglycaemia and her recent home blood pressures are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 25 cm; fetal heart rate 148/min; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.5 mmol/L (ADIPS threshold 5.1); 1 hour 9.8 (10.0); 2 hour 8.4 (8.5); random urine dip negative for ketones

lead_in: How should you interpret and act on this OGTT?

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily today without any glucose monitoring or dietary intervention
options.rationale: First-line GDM management is dietary modification and self-monitored capillary glucose; pharmacotherapy is added when targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2014)

options.text: Order an HbA1c today and only diagnose gestational diabetes if it is at or above 6.5 percent
options.rationale: HbA1c is not used to diagnose GDM; the OGTT is the diagnostic standard in pregnancy per ADIPS. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2014)

options.text: Repeat the OGTT at 30 weeks because two values sit just below the ADIPS cut-offs on this test
options.rationale: One value at or above the ADIPS thresholds diagnoses GDM; her fasting 5.5 exceeds the 5.1 threshold and requires management now. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2014)

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes now on the fasting glucose alone and start dietary and glucose monitoring pathway
options.rationale: The ADIPS diagnostic criteria are fasting 5.1 or above, 1 hour 10.0 or above, or 2 hour 8.5 or above; any one value at or above cut-off diagnoses GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2014)

options.text: Reassure that all values are below WHO diabetes cut-offs and no further action is needed today
options.rationale: ADIPS pregnancy cut-offs (5.1/10.0/8.5) are lower than non-pregnant WHO diabetes cut-offs; her fasting value diagnoses GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2014)

explanation.summary: The ADIPS 2014 consensus (adopted by RANZCOG) diagnoses GDM on a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks with any one of: fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 or above, or 2 hour 8.5 or above. A single elevated value is diagnostic and does not need repeat testing. Initial management is dietary modification and self-monitored capillary blood glucose targeting fasting under 5.0, 1 hour post-meal under 7.4 and 2 hour post-meal under 6.7. Metformin or insulin is added when lifestyle fails to reach targets. HbA1c is used to screen for undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes in early pregnancy but not to diagnose GDM.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds are fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5.
A single value at or above threshold diagnoses GDM.
First-line management is diet and self-monitored capillary glucose.
HbA1c is not diagnostic for GDM.
explanation.pearls: A fasting glucose of 5.1 or above on a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks is enough to diagnose GDM under ADIPS; start diet and capillary glucose monitoring targeting fasting under 5.0 and 2 hour post-meal under 6.7.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

stem:
A 30-year-old woman attends your general practice 4 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding on demand and has not resumed menstruation. Her blood pressure is normal, her BMI is 26 kg/m2, and she is a non-smoker. She has no personal or family history of VTE.

She wants long-acting contraception before returning to sexual activity, hoping to space her next pregnancy by at least 2 to 3 years. She is prepared to consider intrauterine or subdermal options and asks specifically about the effect of any hormonal method on her milk supply.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-healed second-degree perineal tear; uterus not palpable abdominally; lactating breasts with no mastitis
data_table.Investigations: Urine bhCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive plan today?

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM given today with permanent bone density monitoring
options.rationale: DMPA is progestogen-only but reduces bone density over years of use; an implant or IUS is preferred long-acting choice here. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

options.text: Insert a copper IUD today and use condoms for the first 7 days as additional cover
options.rationale: Copper IUD is a good option but the 4 week postpartum window still risks expulsion; the standard IUD insertion window is either within 48 hours or after 4 weeks with cervical assessment. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

options.text: Advise lactational amenorrhoea alone until the baby is 6 months old with no other method needed
options.rationale: LAM is only reliable when all three criteria (fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, under 6 months) apply and she wants active contraception now. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today with 7 days condom use for cover
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum for VTE risk and can reduce milk supply while lactation is being established. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today with no need for additional contraceptive cover
options.rationale: Progestogen-only implant is safe in breastfeeding, does not affect milk supply, and provides immediate contraception when inserted before 21 days postpartum or with LAM criteria met. (Source: FSRH UK MEC; Australian eTG Contraception)

explanation.summary: Postpartum contraception considers VTE risk (elevated for 6 weeks), lactation and future spacing. Progestogen-only methods (mini-pill, subdermal implant, depot, or hormonal IUD) are safe in breastfeeding and do not reduce milk supply. Combined hormonal methods are generally deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum, and longer if VTE risk factors are present or milk supply is not established. Long-acting reversible contraception (implant or IUS) is preferred where possible for spacing preference. IUD insertion is either within 48 hours of birth or after 4 weeks.
key_points: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum.
Progestogen-only methods are safe in lactation and do not reduce milk supply.
IUD insertion is either within 48 hours or after 4 weeks postpartum.
LAM is only reliable under 6 months with full breastfeeding and amenorrhoea.
explanation.pearls: At 4 weeks postpartum in a breastfeeding woman with negative bhCG, an etonogestrel implant is immediately effective and does not affect milk supply; combined pills are deferred until at least 6 weeks.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman (G1P0) at 33+4 weeks presents to birth suite triage with a 3-day frontal headache and blurred vision this morning. She has attended all antenatal appointments and had normal BP throughout. Her booking BMI was 24 kg/m2. On arrival two seated BP readings are 168/112 and 166/108 five minutes apart. She is symptomatic and moderately distressed.

Urine dipstick is 3+ protein and a spot protein:creatinine ratio is 78 mg/mmol. Her platelets are 165 x10^9/L, ALT 34 U/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 145/min with normal variability and no decelerations, and the ultrasound is reassuring. She has taken no antihypertensives.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg then 166/108, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal HR 145/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated; brisk deep tendon reflexes; no clonus; mild bilateral leg oedema; abdomen soft with palpable fetal movements
data_table.Investigations: Urine dip 3+ protein; PCR 78 mg/mmol; platelets 165 x10^9/L; ALT 34 U/L; creatinine 62 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg with a plan to repeat in 30 minutes if BP remains above 160/110
options.rationale: SOMANZ and RANZCOG list oral labetalol as an acceptable first-line agent for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy alongside oral nifedipine and IV hydralazine. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Oral atenolol 50 mg with plans for daily continuation until delivery
options.rationale: Atenolol is associated with fetal growth restriction and is not first-line in acute severe hypertension in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose before any antihypertensive is administered
options.rationale: Magnesium is indicated for seizure prophylaxis with severe pre-eclampsia and is added; it is not itself a BP-lowering agent and should not delay antihypertensive therapy. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg for immediate rapid BP reduction and no monitoring escalation
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine can cause abrupt hypotension and fetal distress; oral immediate-release is the AU recommendation with careful monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

options.text: Oral captopril 12.5 mg with the aim of BP reduction to 130/80 within 1 hour
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to renal teratogenicity and are not used to treat pregnancy hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Pre-eclampsia guideline)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ and RANZCOG guidance for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP 160/110 or above) recommends oral labetalol, oral immediate-release nifedipine, or IV hydralazine as first-line antihypertensives; all three lower BP predictably in the pregnant patient. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading with 1 g/hour maintenance is added for seizure prophylaxis when the diagnosis is severe pre-eclampsia. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and atenolol are avoided in pregnancy. The target is BP below 160/110 with attention to the risk of causing fetal distress if the drop is precipitous.
key_points: First-line antihypertensives are oral labetalol, oral nifedipine, or IV hydralazine.
Sublingual nifedipine risks abrupt hypotension and is not used.
Magnesium is added for seizure prophylaxis, not as an antihypertensive.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs and atenolol are avoided in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: For a BP of 168/112 in pregnancy give oral labetalol 200 mg (or oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release) and add magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; avoid sublingual nifedipine and ACE inhibitors.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to birth suite for a 34-year-old primigravid woman at 40+2 weeks in second stage. The head has just delivered but does not restitute and the shoulders have not descended after 45 seconds despite gentle downward traction. Her BMI is 33 kg/m2 and antenatal ultrasound estimated fetal weight 4.1 kg. The midwife has just called for help and switched on the emergency bell.

Maternal observations remain stable. The mother is in a semi-recumbent position with legs abducted. Fetal heart rate has been reassuring until now and is unavailable at this instant. You are the first doctor at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 96/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, no restitution, chin retracted against perineum (turtle sign); no visible cord
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart rate not currently obtainable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Direct routine episiotomy first regardless of soft tissue distensibility
options.rationale: Episiotomy is considered when it improves internal manoeuvre access, not as a routine first step; the impaction is a bony problem. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the hips and suprapubic pressure applied
options.rationale: RANZCOG algorithm places McRoberts and suprapubic pressure as the first manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia; it resolves 40 to 60 percent of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Fundal pressure applied while continuing axial traction on the fetal head
options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia as it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre to replace the head and proceed to caesarean section
options.rationale: Zavanelli is a last resort after all first- and second-line manoeuvres have failed; it is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

options.text: Deliberate clavicular fracture of the anterior shoulder to reduce the bisacromial diameter
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy or deliberate clavicular fracture is reserved for failure of internal manoeuvres and all-fours position. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is managed with a standardised RANZCOG algorithm summarised by the HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, evaluate for Episiotomy (only if needed to access), Legs (McRoberts) with suprapubic Pressure, then internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, reverse Woods, or delivery of the posterior arm), then Roll to all fours. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy or deliberate clavicular fracture is used only when all standard manoeuvres fail. Fundal pressure is contraindicated because it worsens shoulder impaction and increases risks of brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture. Time to delivery of the shoulders correlates with hypoxic injury risk; the whole sequence generally aims to complete within 5 to 7 minutes.
key_points: McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are first-line and resolve 40 to 60 percent.
Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
Internal manoeuvres and all-fours follow if first-line fails.
Zavanelli, symphysiotomy or clavicular fracture is last resort.
explanation.pearls: For shoulder dystocia the first manoeuvre after calling for help is McRoberts with suprapubic pressure; fundal pressure is contraindicated because it worsens the impaction.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman (G1P0) presents to your regional maternity unit at 32+1 weeks with 3 hours of regular painful contractions every 4 to 5 minutes. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date. On speculum examination her cervix is 3 cm dilated and 80 percent effaced. Fetal fibronectin is not available in your unit. She has not received any antenatal corticosteroids in this pregnancy.

A fetal ultrasound performed on arrival shows a singleton cephalic presentation with an estimated fetal weight of 1.8 kg on the 45th centile. The CTG shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability and no decelerations. Blood pressure is normal, urine is clean. There are no signs of chorioamnionitis and membranes are intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 percent effaced; membranes intact; fetal head engaged
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9 x10^9/L; CRP 4 mg/L; urinalysis clear; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic while corticosteroids and neuroprotection are given?

options.text: Oral indometacin 100 mg loading then 25 mg every 6 hours for a 48 hour course now
options.rationale: Indometacin risks premature ductal closure and oligohydramnios after 32 weeks; nifedipine is preferred at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: No tocolysis; proceed straight to delivery because dilation is beyond 3 cm
options.rationale: Delay of 48 hours for corticosteroid maturation is beneficial at 32 weeks; tocolysis should be attempted concurrently with steroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg loading then 20 mg every 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg in the first hour
options.rationale: RANZCOG and Australian obstetric protocols use oral nifedipine as first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks because of maternal tolerability and evidence for 48 hour delay allowing corticosteroids. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: IV salbutamol infusion at 5 microgram/min titrated to contractions and heart rate
options.rationale: Beta-agonist tocolytics carry unacceptable maternal cardiovascular risk and are second- or third-line only. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

options.text: IV atosiban 6.75 mg bolus then infusion for at least 24 hours as sole tocolytic
options.rationale: Atosiban is effective but more costly and less accessible than nifedipine; it is second-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm labour statement)

explanation.summary: Preterm labour management from 24 to 34 weeks aims to buy 48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids (IM betamethasone 11.4 mg two doses 24 hours apart) and to transfer in utero to a facility with appropriate neonatal care. First-line tocolysis in Australia is oral nifedipine; atosiban is second-line where available. Beta-agonists (salbutamol) are avoided due to maternal cardiovascular risk. Indometacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios. Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks).
key_points: Nifedipine oral is first-line tocolytic at 24 to 34 weeks in Australia.
Indometacin is avoided after 32 weeks for ductal closure risk.
Beta-agonists are avoided for maternal cardiovascular safety.
Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection below 30 weeks (some units to 32 weeks).
explanation.pearls: At 32 weeks in preterm labour give oral nifedipine tocolysis with concurrent IM betamethasone; avoid indometacin (ductal closure) and beta-agonists (cardiovascular risk).

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G2P1) attends your antenatal clinic at 36+2 weeks. Her first pregnancy was an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. On palpation today the fetus feels breech and this is confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound: a frank breech, fetal back on the maternal left, adequate amniotic fluid volume and an anterior placenta clear of the lower segment. Estimated fetal weight is 2.9 kg on the 55th centile.

She has no scars on her uterus, no antepartum haemorrhage in this pregnancy, no known fetal abnormality and no evidence of ruptured membranes. Her booking BMI was 26 kg/m2 and her blood pressure has remained normal throughout. She wants to avoid caesarean if possible and asks about your recommendation for the next 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 34 cm; frank breech confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound; adequate amniotic fluid; no palpable uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: EFW 2.9 kg (55th centile); anterior placenta clear of lower segment; normal amniotic fluid index

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation now?

options.text: Recommend vaginal breech delivery at 40 weeks without any attempt at ECV as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Vaginal breech is only offered in selected women with strict criteria and experienced operator; ECV is offered first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Advise moxibustion at the outer little toe alone as the primary intervention until 39 weeks
options.rationale: Moxibustion has limited evidence and is not a substitute for offering ECV in a formal maternity setting. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Perform ECV in the outpatient clinic today at 36+2 without tocolysis or CTG monitoring
options.rationale: ECV should be performed from 37 weeks in a facility with capacity for immediate caesarean if needed and with CTG monitoring; earlier attempts have higher spontaneous version rates that make procedure unnecessary. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis and continuous fetal monitoring in the birth suite
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends ECV from 37 weeks in eligible women with singleton term breech to reduce caesarean rate; her situation has no contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

options.text: Book elective caesarean section for 39 weeks without discussing external cephalic version
options.rationale: ECV should be offered first in eligible women because a successful version returns her to routine cephalic vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Management of breech statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG recommends offering external cephalic version from 37 weeks in women with singleton term breech and no contraindications (previous caesarean scar being a relative contraindication, plus antepartum haemorrhage, placenta praevia, oligohydramnios, fetal abnormality, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy). ECV is done in a facility with immediate access to caesarean, with tocolysis (typically nifedipine or salbutamol) and continuous CTG. Success rates are 50 to 60 percent in multiparous women and 30 to 40 percent in nulliparous women. Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women within 72 hours of ECV. Vaginal breech delivery is offered only when strict RANZCOG criteria are met with experienced practitioners.
key_points: ECV is first-line for term breech in eligible women.
Performed from 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG in a birth-ready setting.
Anti-D within 72 hours in Rh-negative women.
Vaginal breech delivery has strict operator and criteria requirements.
explanation.pearls: For a G2P1 with singleton frank breech at 36+2 weeks and no contraindications, offer ECV at 37 weeks with tocolysis and CTG monitoring; anti-D within 72 hours if Rh negative.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on-call and are called urgently at 03:15 to a 28-year-old multipara at 39+5 weeks in the birth suite. She has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes with a moderate gush of clear liquor. The midwife immediately palpates a soft pulsatile cord in the vagina at the introitus. The CTG shows a prolonged fetal deceleration to 80/min for the last 3 minutes with poor variability, having previously been reactive.

The patient is a spontaneous labourer with cervix now 6 cm dilated, fetal head at the pelvic inlet, station -2. Full theatre team is stood by and anaesthetist is 8 minutes away by phone. She has been prepared for anaesthesia (fasting 6 hours). She has no significant medical history and no cardiovascular contraindications.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 100/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 80/min for 3 minutes
data_table.Examination: Cord palpable and pulsating at introitus; cervix 6 cm dilated; head at -2 station; membranes ruptured
data_table.Investigations: Group and save on file; last Hb 128 g/L (115-160); no pre-existing coagulopathy

lead_in: Which single set of pre-transfer measures should you undertake now to maximise fetal survival before theatre?

options.text: Reduce the cord back through the cervix with a warm saline soaked pack and continue augmentation of labour with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Cord replacement is not routine; it risks cord damage and delays delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Continue oxytocin augmentation to achieve rapid vaginal delivery of the head while she is still 6 cm with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Oxytocin worsens compression by contracting uterus; the immediate need is delivery by category-1 caesarean unless immediate vaginal birth is possible. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Apply Kielland forceps to expedite vaginal delivery from -2 station with pudendal block only with standard supportive measures alongside
options.rationale: Instrumental delivery requires the head at or below the ischial spines with cervix fully dilated; -2 station at 6 cm is not amenable. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Perform emergency symphysiotomy in the birth suite while awaiting the anaesthetist to arrive with standard supportive measures alongside
options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is not part of the AU cord prolapse pathway; category-1 caesarean is the definitive management. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

options.text: Elevate the presenting part manually and place her in knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position with a filled 500 mL bladder catheter and IV tocolysis if delivery is likely delayed
options.rationale: RANZCOG cord prolapse pathway uses manual elevation, positioning to relieve compression, bladder filling and tocolysis while transferring urgently to theatre for delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical cord prolapse statement)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is a category-1 obstetric emergency requiring delivery within 30 minutes (target 15 to 20). The immediate holding measures are: (1) manually elevate the presenting part with two fingers in the vagina to relieve cord compression, keep the fingers in place during transfer if possible; (2) position the mother in knee-chest, exaggerated Sims or Trendelenburg; (3) fill the bladder with 500 mL warmed saline via Foley catheter (raises the presenting part when manual elevation cannot be maintained); (4) start IV tocolysis (nifedipine or terbutaline) if delivery is likely to be delayed. Vaginal delivery is only pursued if the cervix is fully dilated with the head at or below spines. Category-1 caesarean is otherwise definitive. The cord should be kept warm and moist without excessive handling; do not attempt to reposition it above the cervix.
key_points: Manual elevation of presenting part is first-line during transfer.
Bladder filling with 500 mL saline relieves compression when hands must be freed.
Tocolysis buys time if there is any transfer delay.
Category-1 caesarean is definitive unless immediate vaginal delivery is possible.
explanation.pearls: In cord prolapse elevate the presenting part manually, fill the bladder with 500 mL saline, position in knee-chest and give tocolysis; deliver by category-1 caesarean within 30 minutes unless the cervix is fully dilated and head is at or below spines.

stem:
You are the O and G registrar in a metropolitan tertiary hospital. A 34-year-old woman (G4P3) delivered a 4.3 kg baby 45 minutes ago after a spontaneous labour induced for postdates. She had a manually removed placenta for retained placenta. Her booking bloods showed normal Hb and platelets. She has ongoing haemorrhage now totalling 2500 mL despite: Syntocinon 10 unit IM at delivery, Syntocinon 40 unit infusion running, ergometrine 250 microgram IM after 15 minutes, carboprost 250 microgram IM after 25 minutes, misoprostol 800 microgram PR, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression, empty bladder, and 2 units of packed cells running.

Her uterus remains soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum inspection is negative for genital tract trauma. Coagulation testing 10 minutes ago showed fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, temperature 35.4 degrees C. Consultant is 15 minutes away. Theatre is available now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on 6 L oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, 2 cm above umbilicus; no visible genital tract trauma on speculum; bladder empty via IDC
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5); platelets 78 x10^9/L; INR 1.4; venous lactate 4.6 mmol/L; running 2 units PRBC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step now?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with continued transfusion and activation of massive transfusion protocol
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH management escalates to mechanical tamponade (Bakri balloon) after pharmacological failure while blood product resuscitation continues; MTP activation covers ongoing coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; National Blood Authority MTP)

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes until 8 doses are given regardless of hypertension
options.rationale: Carboprost is capped at 8 doses in total but tone-directed pharmacological therapy has already failed here; mechanical measures are indicated. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Repeat tranexamic acid 1 g IV every 30 minutes without other escalation until bleeding stops as the sole intervention
options.rationale: A second TXA dose is given at 30 minutes if bleeding continues, but escalation to mechanical and surgical measures should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Immediate hysterectomy in the birth suite without prior balloon tamponade or interventional radiology
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but is generally preceded by balloon tamponade or uterine compression sutures; jumping to hysterectomy skips reversible mechanical measures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

options.text: Continue current transfusion at the current rate and observe for another 30 minutes before further action
options.rationale: Ongoing haemorrhage above 2 litres with hypotension and coagulopathy requires immediate escalation, not observation. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: In refractory PPH after full pharmacological uterotonic escalation (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol), the RANZCOG pathway moves to mechanical measures - intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri, Rusch or Foley) - with concurrent blood product resuscitation. Massive transfusion protocol should be activated for ongoing losses above 40 percent blood volume with hypotension or coagulopathy; NBA guidance uses 1:1:1 ratios of PRBC, FFP and platelets with early cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L. Warm the patient (hypothermia worsens coagulation). If balloon tamponade fails, surgical options are B-Lynch or other compression sutures, then internal iliac artery ligation or uterine artery embolisation, then hysterectomy as the definitive step. Balancing correction of the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) continues throughout.
key_points: After pharmacological failure move to balloon tamponade with continued transfusion.
Activate MTP for >40 percent blood volume loss with hypotension or coagulopathy.
Cryoprecipitate is added early when fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L.
Hysterectomy is the definitive final step if mechanical and other surgical measures fail.
explanation.pearls: After maximal uterotonic therapy fails in PPH, transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with concurrent massive transfusion protocol activation, cryoprecipitate replacement of low fibrinogen, active warming and preparation for surgical compression sutures.

stem:
You are the GP shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old woman at 27 weeks gestation with her first pregnancy. She has no personal history of diabetes but her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. Her booking BMI was 29 kg/m2. She has had no antenatal complications so far and fetal movements are normal.

Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks reports fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour plasma glucose 9.6 mmol/L and 2 hour plasma glucose 8.3 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic. Fetal biometry today shows growth appropriate for gestation with an abdominal circumference on the 60th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symphyseal-fundal height 27 cm, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.3 mmol/L (<8.5); HbA1c 5.6 percent

lead_in: Which of the following best describes the interpretation and next management step?

options.text: Normal OGTT; continue routine antenatal care and repeat OGTT only if polyhydramnios or macrosomia develops later
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS diagnostic threshold of 5.1 mmol/L so this is diagnostic of GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance; repeat OGTT at 32 weeks and defer any dietary intervention until that repeat test
options.rationale: ADIPS uses single-threshold criteria on any of the three values; there is no intermediate impaired glucose tolerance category diagnosed antenatally. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: Overt diabetes in pregnancy; start immediate insulin therapy without a trial of lifestyle and dietary modification
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting 7.0 or higher, random 11.1 or higher, HbA1c 6.5 percent or higher; none apply so this is GDM, not overt diabetes. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: GDM; refer to a diabetes-in-pregnancy service, start diet and lifestyle change and begin glucose self-monitoring
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS threshold; management is multidisciplinary with diet and exercise, self-monitoring and metformin or insulin if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: GDM; commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line without an initial dietary trial period
options.rationale: Initial management of GDM is a dietary and exercise trial with self-monitoring; pharmacotherapy begins if targets not achieved after 1 to 2 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

explanation.summary: The ADIPS 75 g OGTT diagnostic thresholds for GDM at 24-28 weeks are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher. Any single value meets diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by fasting 7.0 mmol/L or higher, random 11.1 mmol/L or higher, or HbA1c 6.5 percent or higher and requires immediate specialist input. GDM initial management is lifestyle modification plus 1-2 week trial with self-monitoring targets fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L. If targets not met, metformin or insulin is added; insulin remains the mainstay for tight fasting control.
key_points: ADIPS fasting threshold for GDM is 5.1 mmol/L; 1 hr 10.0; 2 hr 8.5.
Any single value exceeding threshold diagnoses GDM.
First-line is diet, exercise and self-monitoring for 1-2 weeks.
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS GDM thresholds on 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; any one value at threshold diagnoses GDM.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

subtopic_detail: Advice for future pregnancies after a baby with early onset sepsis
stem: A 32-year-old woman attends for a debrief six weeks after her first baby was treated in the neonatal unit. She asks what would be different in a future pregnancy.

data_table.Index birth: Term vaginal birth, blood culture on day one grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Today: Mother and baby both well, no allergies, no other complications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She will be offered antibiotics in every future labour whatever a swab shows
options.rationale: A previous infant with invasive disease is a standing indication that does not depend on later screening results. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.text: She will be swabbed at 36 weeks and treated only if that swab is positive
options.rationale: Screening decides the plan for a woman with no standing indication, which no longer describes her. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.text: She will be offered a planned caesarean section to avoid the birth canal
options.rationale: Caesarean is chosen for obstetric reasons and is not a means of preventing this infection. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.text: She will need an oral antibiotic through the whole third trimester next time
options.rationale: Prolonged oral treatment has no role here, though a significant bacteriuria found next time would be treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.text: Nothing changes, because this was a single event unlikely to happen again
options.rationale: That reassurance fits a mother who was merely colonised, not one whose infant had invasive disease. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

explanation.summary: A previous infant with invasive group B streptococcal disease marks a woman as having a persistently high genital tract load or an infant-level susceptibility, and the recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy is high enough that Australian guidance makes intrapartum prophylaxis automatic. She is not swabbed at 35 to 37 weeks, because a negative result would not change the plan and risks misleading the birth suite team. The same override applies to significant group B streptococcal bacteriuria in the index pregnancy. Postnatal debriefing after a neonatal unit admission is also the moment to talk through what happened, to document the standing indication clearly in her record, and to offer psychological support where the admission was distressing. In context, clear documentation is what turns this piece of history into an antibiotic actually given during the next labour.
key_points: A previous infant with invasive disease is a standing indication in every later pregnancy.
No 35 to 37 week swab is needed once that indication exists.
Caesarean section is not a preventive strategy for this infection.
Document the indication prominently so the birth suite team acts on it.
explanation.pearls: Postnatal debriefing after a neonatal unit admission is also a screening opportunity for perinatal anxiety and post-traumatic symptoms, which are common after an unexpected separation from the baby.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

stem:
You are the on-call registrar. A 31-year-old woman with severe pre-eclampsia has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks. She had labetalol running throughout and her most recent blood pressure was 158/102 mmHg. Placenta was delivered spontaneously and appears complete on inspection. Estimated blood loss so far is 1200 mL and continues to flow briskly.

On examination the fundus is boggy but there is no obvious trauma. Bimanual compression is initiated by your midwifery colleague and intravenous access is confirmed patent. Uterine massage produces a small transient contraction. Bloods are being sent. The patient is alert and speaking but pale. IV oxytocin 10 units has been given as part of active management and a further 40 units infusion in 1 litre normal saline is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, no visible tear on speculum, moderate ongoing dark blood loss, bimanual compression in progress
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing; Hb pending; group and hold sent; coagulation panel pending

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next agent given her clinical picture?

options.text: Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive women; carboprost is the appropriate escalation when oxytocin is already running and hypertension precludes ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular repeat once as second-line agent after ongoing oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it precipitates hypertensive crisis. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Syntometrine 1 mL intramuscular containing 5 units oxytocin and 500 microgram ergometrine combined
options.rationale: Syntometrine contains ergometrine and is contraindicated in hypertension for the same reason. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual and re-dose at 60 minutes if bleeding persists
options.rationale: Misoprostol is an option in resource-poor settings; in Australian tertiary units carboprost is preferred second-line for atony refractory to oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous as monotherapy in place of additional uterotonic agents
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is a valuable adjunct to uterotonics but does not replace an additional uterotonic when uterine atony continues. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of vaginal birth (1000 mL for caesarean), most commonly from uterine atony. Management combines bimanual compression and bladder emptying, uterotonic escalation, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of onset, and blood product resuscitation. Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because they trigger hypertensive crisis, so the escalation ladder skips to carboprost intramuscularly. Misoprostol is used where carboprost is unavailable, and refractory bleeding leads to balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation or surgery.
key_points: Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia.
Carboprost is the appropriate second-line agent after oxytocin in these patients.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given within 3 hours of onset as adjunct.
Consider balloon tamponade or surgery for refractory bleeding.
explanation.pearls: In postpartum haemorrhage with hypertension or pre-eclampsia, skip ergometrine and syntometrine and escalate directly from oxytocin to carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 30+2 weeks gestation from a rural transfer with regular painful contractions for 4 hours. Speculum shows cervix 3 cm dilated with intact membranes. Fetal fibronectin was positive on the referring hospital assessment. She has no vaginal bleeding, no fever and no history of asthma. Booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg and today's is 118/72 mmHg. Fetal heart rate on continuous cardiotocography is reassuring with baseline 145/min and normal variability.

She has already received the first dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg. Neonatal intensive care is available on site. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is being prepared. She has no drug allergies and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Regular contractions every 3 minutes; cervix 3 cm dilated 60 percent effaced; membranes intact; cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Fetal fibronectin positive; fetal cardiotocography baseline 145/min normal variability; full blood count within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: Which tocolytic is the most appropriate first-line choice to buy time for corticosteroid completion and transfer?

options.text: Salbutamol 100 microgram intravenous infusion titrated to slow contractions over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Beta agonists cause significant maternal cardiovascular side effects and are no longer preferred first-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg oral immediate release stat, then 20 mg every 30 minutes for two further doses if contractions persist
options.rationale: Nifedipine is the first-line tocolytic in Australian practice with a favourable maternal safety profile and equivalent efficacy to atosiban. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Atosiban 6.75 mg intravenous bolus then 300 microgram per minute infusion for 3 hours as first-line agent
options.rationale: Atosiban is effective but is not typically first-line in Australia due to cost; nifedipine is preferred initial choice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Indometacin 100 mg per rectum then 25 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours as tocolysis regardless of the gestation involved
options.rationale: Indometacin is used only under 32 weeks for limited duration due to premature ductus arteriosus closure risk; nifedipine is broader-use first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose then 1 g per hour as combined tocolysis and neuroprotection
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection under 30 weeks but is not effective as a tocolytic; a separate tocolytic is required. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

explanation.summary: The aim of tocolysis in preterm labour is to delay delivery by 48 hours so antenatal corticosteroids can act and in-utero transfer can occur if required. Nifedipine is the Australian first-line agent based on efficacy equivalent to atosiban, oral administration, low cost and acceptable side-effect profile. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular is given as two doses 24 hours apart when delivery is anticipated between 24 and 34+6 weeks. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is used at gestations under 30 weeks; indometacin is reserved for gestations under 32 weeks for up to 48 hours.
key_points: Nifedipine is the Australian first-line tocolytic in preterm labour.
Aim is 48 hours delay for antenatal steroid effect and transfer.
Magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective, not tocolytic, and used under 30 weeks.
Indometacin only under 32 weeks and limited to 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: For preterm labour under 34 weeks in Australia, first-line tocolysis is nifedipine 20 mg oral stat then titrated dosing to buy 48 hours for corticosteroid effect.

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a G3P1 obstetric history presents to your gynaecology emergency clinic with right-sided pelvic pain and light PV spotting for 24 hours. Her last menstrual period was 6+3 weeks ago. Two years ago she had a laparoscopic left salpingectomy for a ruptured left tubal ectopic. She and her partner have been actively trying to conceive for the past 8 months. She is haemodynamically stable and has no shoulder tip pain.

On examination she has right adnexal tenderness without peritonism. Her serum beta hCG is 3200 IU/L today, and a repeat 48 hours ago was 1900 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows an empty uterus with an endometrium of 12 mm, a 2.4 cm right tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity and a small amount of free pelvic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Full blood count and coagulation are within normal limits. She has no significant medical history and no allergies. Her body surface area is calculated at 1.75 m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right adnexal tenderness without peritonism; cervix closed on speculum; scant blood in vagina; no shoulder tip pain
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 3200 IU/L (today) rising from 1900 IU/L (48 hours ago); TVUS empty uterus, right tubal 2.4 cm mass no cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas free fluid; Hb 128 g/L (115-165); coagulation within normal limits; body surface area 1.75 m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Expectant management with beta hCG surveillance twice weekly aiming for spontaneous resolution over 2-4 weeks
options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling beta hCG and small mass; her beta hCG is rising which excludes this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area with day 4 and 7 beta hCG
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a reasonable option (mass under 3.5 cm, beta hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, no significant pain), but with the contralateral tube already lost, preserving fertility takes priority; conservative surgical salpingostomy is preferred over medical management here to allow future ipsilateral tubal function without waiting weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with careful haemostasis and post-operative beta hCG surveillance
options.rationale: With prior contralateral salpingectomy the right tube is her only tube; conservative salpingostomy preserves tubal patency while removing the ectopic and gives the best chance of future spontaneous conception. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy as definitive treatment given the ectopic in the sole remaining tube
options.rationale: Salpingectomy on the sole remaining tube commits her to IVF; salpingostomy preserves tubal function and is preferred if technically feasible in this context. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Ultrasound-guided intra-sac methotrexate injection under transvaginal guidance today
options.rationale: Direct sac injection is used for cornual or interstitial ectopic; standard tubal ectopic is managed medically with systemic methotrexate or surgically. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy include beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, reliable follow-up and no contraindications (renal or hepatic dysfunction, blood dyscrasia, breastfeeding, active pulmonary or peptic ulcer disease, immunodeficiency). Salpingectomy is preferred when the contralateral tube is healthy because recurrence risk after salpingostomy in the same tube is higher than a new ectopic in a normal contralateral tube. However, when the contralateral tube has already been removed or is grossly diseased, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility. Methotrexate is an alternative when surgery is declined but has a longer resolution timeline and lower success in the setting.
key_points: Salpingectomy is preferred when contralateral tube is healthy.
Salpingostomy is preferred when contralateral tube is absent or diseased.
Methotrexate requires beta hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm and no cardiac activity.
Direct sac injection is reserved for cornual or interstitial ectopics.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts the usual salpingectomy-vs-salpingostomy preference: preserve the only remaining tube with salpingostomy where technically feasible.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 at 33+4 weeks gestation admitted overnight with hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg. Overnight she has developed severe headache resistant to paracetamol, epigastric pain and reduced urine output. She has had no seizures. Fetal movements are reduced. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 155/min with reduced variability but no decelerations.

Investigations show blood pressure 168/112 mmHg after two doses of intravenous labetalol 20 mg. Platelets are 82 x10^9/L (150-450), creatinine has risen from 62 micromol/L at booking to 118 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 148 U/L (<45), urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30). Urine output has been 25 mL/hour for the last 4 hours. A 4 g intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose was completed 30 minutes ago and the 1 g/hour infusion is running. Her partner is at the bedside. Fetal biometry today shows growth on the 15th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, fetal HR 155/min
data_table.Examination: Alert but distressed, brisk deep tendon reflexes without clonus, right upper quadrant tenderness, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, symphysio-fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90) rising from 62; ALT 148 U/L (<45); urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30); urine output 25 mL/h for 4 hours; CTG baseline 155/min reduced variability

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue intravenous labetalol and reassess blood pressure and urine output in another 2 hours before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: Her rising creatinine, rising liver enzymes and severe headache are SOMANZ deterioration features; waiting another 2 hours delays the decision to plan birth. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)
